transcript.text: Worcester Greenstar 30i combi - pressure keeps dropping to about 0.5 bar every few days and I have to top it up. Can you help me work out why?

Losing that much pressure every few days means water is escaping from the sealed system somewhere. Here's how to narrow it down.

## Quick background
• Normal cold pressure on a Greenstar 30i is about 1–1.5 bar. When the heating is running it typically rises to around 1.5–2 bar.
• The pressure relief valve (PRV) opens at 3 bar to protect the boiler.
• The water has to be going to one of three places: a leak in the pipework or radiators, out through the PRV, or a leak inside the boiler.

## Step 1: Watch the gauge hot vs cold (the most useful test)
Top up to about 1.2 bar with the system cold, then run the heating for 30–60 minutes and check the gauge.

• It climbs to 2.5–3 bar when hot: This strongly suggests the expansion vessel has lost its air charge. The water has nowhere to expand, so the pressure spikes, the PRV dumps water, and it drops back low when it cools. This is probably the most common cause on boilers a few years old.
• It rises only modestly (to about 1.5–2 bar): The expansion vessel is probably fine, so a leak is more likely.

## Step 2: Check the PRV discharge pipe
Look for a copper pipe (usually 15mm) coming from the bottom of the boiler, going through the wall, and ending outside, often pointing down at the wall or a drain.
• Look for drips, wet patches, staining, or green/white crusty deposits at the end.
• Tie a small plastic bag over the end (or put a container under it) for a few days. If water collects, the PRV is releasing. That's caused either by the expansion vessel problem above or by a worn PRV that weeps even at normal pressure.

## Step 3: Hunt for leaks
• Under the boiler: Check for drips, damp, or crusty deposits on the valves and pipes.
• Every radiator: Check the valves, TRV heads, bleed screws, and joints. Wipe them with dry kitchen roll, since slow weeps often just evaporate and leave brown or white crusty marks rather than puddles.
• Pipework: Check exposed pipes, airing cupboards, and under sinks.
• Hidden signs: Look for damp patches on ceilings, stained floorboards, swollen skirting, or musty smells. Pipes under floors or in screed can leak unseen.
• Did you bleed radiators recently? If so, a small drop afterward is normal. But a repeated drop every few days isn't.

## Step 4: Boiler on vs off
Turn the heating off (or the boiler off) for 24–48 hours with the pressure at about 1.2 bar.
• It still drops while cold and off: You have a genuine leak somewhere in the system.
• It only drops when the heating has been running: This points to the expansion vessel or PRV.

## What the fixes usually involve
• Expansion vessel recharge: The vessel sits inside the boiler casing. An engineer depressurises the system and pumps it back up to about 0.75–1 bar via its valve. This is cheap and quick if the vessel's diaphragm is intact. If the diaphragm has failed (water comes out of the valve), the vessel needs replacing.
• PRV replacement: If the PRV is weeping at normal pressure, it needs replacing. Also a fairly routine job.
• Radiator valve or joint leaks: Often a simple tighten or repack, which a confident DIYer can sometimes do.
• Internal boiler leak: This needs an engineer.

Anything inside the boiler casing must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer. The 30i case is room-sealed, so please don't remove it yourself.

## Worth knowing
• Check your warranty. Worcester often gives 5–10+ years if the boiler was registered and serviced annually. Call Worcester Bosch first, because the repair may be free.
• Don't keep topping up long term. Each top-up brings in fresh, oxygen-rich water and dilutes the corrosion inhibitor, which speeds up internal rusting and sludge.
• Leak sealers (e.g., Fernox LS-X) can fix tiny, inaccessible weeps. But use them only once you've ruled out the PRV and expansion vessel, and check they won't affect your warranty.

If you can tell me what the gauge does when the heating's on, and whether there's any sign of water at the outside discharge pipe, I can help you narrow it down further.

When the heating's on full the pressure goes up to nearly 3 bar, then drops back afterwards. The little copper pipe outside the wall does drip sometimes, more when the heating's on. No gas smell and my CO alarm is quiet.

That pattern points almost certainly to a failed or flat expansion vessel.

## What's happening
1. The expansion vessel has a sealed air cushion that absorbs the extra volume when water heats up. Over time that air charge leaks away.
2. Without it, the water has nowhere to go when it heats, so the pressure shoots up towards 3 bar.
3. The pressure relief valve opens at about 3 bar and dumps water out of the copper pipe. That's the drip you're seeing, and it's the safety system working as designed.
4. When the system cools, there's now less water in it, so the pressure falls to about 0.5 bar.
5. You top up, and the cycle repeats.

The no gas smell and quiet CO alarm are reassuring, but this fault is on the water side and is unrelated to gas or combustion.

## What needs doing
Get a Gas Safe registered engineer. On the Greenstar 30i the expansion vessel is inside the boiler casing. The casing forms part of the sealed combustion chamber, so you shouldn't remove it yourself.

They'll typically:
• Recharge the vessel. They'll drop the system pressure to zero, then pump the vessel back up to its set pressure, usually around 0.75–1 bar. This is often a quick job.
• Replace the vessel if the internal diaphragm has split. A giveaway is water coming out of the vessel's air valve instead of air. On some Greenstar models this is a bigger job, and an external vessel is sometimes fitted instead.
• Check or replace the PRV. After repeatedly discharging, PRVs often pick up debris and keep weeping even at normal pressure. It's worth asking them to check it while they're there.
• Check the inhibitor level. All that fresh top-up water dilutes the corrosion inhibitor and adds oxygen to the system, so a top-up of inhibitor is a good idea.

Rough UK costs: a recharge is often about £80–150, and a vessel or PRV replacement more like £150–350 including labour. Prices vary by area.

## Before you book
• Check your warranty. Worcester often gives 5–10+ years if the boiler was registered and serviced annually. Call Worcester Bosch with your serial number, since this repair may be free.
• If you have boiler cover (British Gas, HomeServe, etc.), this should normally be included.

## In the meantime
• Top up to about 1 bar when cold, not higher. The more you start with, the sooner it hits 3 bar.
• Don't leave it sitting below about 0.5 bar, as the boiler may lock out.
• Turning the heating down a bit can reduce how often the PRV discharges.
• Don't block or cap the discharge pipe.

It's a common, fixable fault, but worth sorting reasonably soon so you're not constantly adding fresh water and wearing out the PRV.
